messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 55
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Fashion Designer
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 41

Elias, fifty-five, sits on the edge of the studio chair, fingers tracing the grain of the oak table. His workshop smells of steam, raw wool, and the sharp tang of tailor’s chalk. He has always worked with his hands. The memory surfaces unbidden when the studio door catches on the floorboards—a sudden, metallic scrape that mirrors the back door slamming in his childhood home. He is seven again. The air in that hallway is thick with whiskey and unspooled rage. The first strike catches his ribs. He does not cry out. He learns that stillness is safer than movement. The second blow sends him against the plaster. He counts the floorboards beneath his palm. One, two, three. He learns to shrink himself, to make his bones smaller than they are. He carries that calculation into his twenties, then his thirties, then now. He builds clothes that structure the body, that armor the frame. His collections are sharp-shouldered coats, structured blazers, tailoring that leaves no room for collapse. When he pins fabric to the dress form, he smooths every seam with deliberate pressure. Control is the craft. He married young, drawn to warmth, but the wariness he mistook for practicality kept him distant. His divorce was amicable, mostly, though he never explains why he left first. He learned, quietly, that closeness often precedes the strike. He works now in a converted warehouse in Montreal, surrounded by bolts of fabric and half-formed silhouettes. His assistants know not to touch his sketches. They know not to enter the space without knocking twice. Today, he sits in the therapy office, which has softer lighting than his studio. He wears a dark turtleneck, sleeves pulled slightly forward, wrists crossed over his knees. When the wall clock ticks past the hour, his shoulders rise a fraction. He says he cannot sleep through the night. Sleep requires surrender. Instead, he wakes at 3:14 a.m., every night, his body already braced for impact. He checks the door locks three times, testing the deadbolt with his palm, feeling for resistance. At work, he becomes frantic when a client questions a pattern draft. He will erase a line, then redraw it, then cut the muslin entirely. He says he needs the material to obey him. He admits that flinching happens without warning. A raised hand in a grocery store aisle sends his vision narrowing to a tunnel. He has left carts mid-aisle, heart hammering against his sternum, the old floorboards counting behind his eyes. He sketches at his desk during the session sometimes, charcoal smudging his fingertips. The lines begin tight, then loosen as he speaks. He tells the clinician about the nightmares, though he calls them technical rehearsals. He describes the way his stomach knots before he enters any room with a door that closes behind him. He notes that he avoids mirrors when he is angry, afraid he will recognize his father’s posture in his own reflection. He does not speak of the violence in detail. He speaks of the weight, the sound, the geometry of survival. He says he feels exhausted from carrying a body that still believes it is being hunted. He sets his pencil down. The studio will wait. The fabric will wait. He breathes, slowly, and watches the dust settle on the windowsill, waiting for the next hour to pass.
